Junfeng Ni, Ziyu Zhu, Fan Jiang, Yu Liu, Chiyu Wang, Jiawei Zhang, Zhaoxu Sun, Mu Xu, Siyuan Huang, Yixin Chen
Video diffusion models generate visually compelling short-term sequences but often struggle to preserve scene geometry and object structure over time. In this paper, we first demonstrate that current video attention cannot identify reliable correspondences across frames, with responses dispersed across multiple regions even after recognizable scene structure has emerged. We argue that reliable cross-frame associations are essential for information exchange as scene structure forms in video generation. Thus, we introduce Geometry Attention Distillation (GAD), which transfers correspondences from a frozen geometry model's attention to video attention. Extracted from clean videos, these correspondences link the same static surface or moving object across frames. Since structure formation begins in deeper layers at higher noise and shallower layers at lower noise, we apply attention distillation at a student layer selected according to the noise timestep. After training, video attention focuses more consistently on corresponding locations. Experiments across all three video backbones demonstrate improved long-range scene consistency and dynamic temporal consistency, with geometric gains across generation lengths. On Wan2.2 5B, GAD improves cross-frame matching accuracy by at least 30% over the Wan baseline on both long-range benchmarks. Notably, GAD achieves these gains without additional inference modules, offering a promising approach to efficient and consistent video-based world simulation. Project page: https://fantasy-amap.github.io/GAD/.
comment: Project page: https://fantasy-amap.github.io/GAD/
☆ The Federated Tumor Segmentation and Classification (FeTS++) Challenge
Wenyi Tang, Carla Pitarch-Abaigar, Siddhesh Thakur, Verena Chung, Konstantinos Koukoutegos, Alexandros Karargyris, Holger R. Roth, Spyridon Bakas
International challenges have become the standard for developing and benchmarking biomedical image analysis methods using centralized multi-institutional data. Federated learning (FL) describes a paradigm-shift on multi-institutional collaborations, where models are trained across institutions while their data are always retained locally. The Federated Tumor Segmentation (FeTS) challenge, first held in 2021, was the first challenge dedicated to FL in medical imaging and editions in 2022 and 2024 pushed the frontiers of real-world method validation. FeTS++ 2027 returns after a two-year gap with a substantially larger and more diverse cohort, and with the two "pluses" that name the challenge: an official classification task alongside segmentation, and a move of the infrastructure to NVIDIA FLARE (NVFlare). Built on the clinically acquired, multi-institutional multi-parametric MRI data of the BraTS 2025 Lighthouse challenge, FeTS++ spans gliomas and meningiomas across patient cohorts from institutions in North America, Europe, Asia, and Africa, and focuses on ranking submitted methodological approaches according to their model utility and an efficiency-aware score. Task 1 asks participants to find the best strategy for aggregating knowledge from per-institution segmentation models, while Task 2 asks them to distinguish glioma from meningioma under the same federated protocol, in which the entity label is heavily confounded with the site of origin.

Koushik Howlader, Tirtho Roy, Md Tauhidul Islam, Wei Le
Predicting spatial gene expression from standard H&E images could extend molecular analysis to tissues without spatial transcriptomic measurements. A standard Transformer applies self-attention over spots but ignores where each spot sits in the tissue, whereas a spot's molecular state depends on tissue context at multiple spatial scales. Building on this insight, we introduce MIST, a Multi-context Spatial Transformer that augments the self-attention backbone with two context pathways applied in every layer: a coordinate-invariant local pathway that attends over spatial k-nearest-neighbor spots, and a slide pathway that broadcasts a whole-slide summary to every spot; the model predicts all spots in a single forward pass. Because coordinates enter only through pairwise distances, the local pathway is invariant to translations, rotations, and reflections when image features are fixed. In intra-cohort evaluation across six human organ cohorts from HEST-1k, MIST improves mean Pearson correlation over the strongest evaluated baseline by 9.7%, 11.6%, and 11.4% for 10-, 50-, and 100-gene panels, respectively, with the lowest average MSE and MAE. MIST further improves leave-one-organ-out transfer by 6.0% over the next strongest baseline, attains the best expression-derived domain recovery (highest mean ARI and NMI at every clustering resolution, and higher NMI than the closest baseline on 84% of held-out slides), and reproduces spatial expression patterns of selected cancer-marker genes. Together, these results show that adding local and slide context to a vanilla Transformer backbone is an effective approach to spatial gene expression prediction from histology.
☆ LayerCanvas: Infographic Generation in AI Learning Assistants via Hybrid Layer-Set Diffusion
Keshav Gupta, Jeremy Owen, Christopher Lloyd, Shaunak Mishra, Manav Sharma
Online learning platforms are increasingly deploying AI assistants to provide personalized, on-demand tutoring. These can leverage infographics to communicate complex information and improve the learning experience. However, automating effective infographic generation remains a challenging task, requiring a combination of visual richness with precise typography, structured layouts, and continued editability. Existing representation methods satisfy these goals only in part: Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) representations preserve geometry, hierarchy, and text but provide limited aesthetic flexibility, while raster diffusion models produce richer appearances by flattening content and layout into a single image. Conditioning a diffusion model on a rasterized SVG does not resolve this conflict because the raster preserves approximate placement but discards element ownership, occlusion relationships, and the structure needed to modify and recompose the result. We introduce LayerCanvas, a hybrid approach that retains SVG as the semantic, structural, and typographic program while using diffusion to aestheticize non-text content. Rather than generating one flattened raster, LayerCanvas partitions SVG elements into z-ordered sets of mutually non-overlapping elements and processes them through communicating parallel RGB generation streams. The resulting layers are independently editable and deterministically recomposed, while text is rendered from preserved vector metadata. Our approach combines rich visual synthesis with accurate typography and localized editing. LayerCanvas substantially improves text fidelity over state-of-the-art raster image generators while achieving the highest overall aesthetic quality. We further demonstrate non-destructive content editing, localization, asset reuse, and animation.

Arunachalam Venkatachalam, Mhafuzul Islam, Marwan Yusuf, David Van Hamme, Ben Stoffelen, James Foresi
Reliable detection of pedestrians and road users is essential for the safe operation of autonomous vehicles. However, this task becomes increasingly challenging under adverse environmental conditions, such as poor weather and low lighting, where the performance of state-of-the-art pre-trained object detectors and on-board sensors tends to degrade, which limits their effectiveness and reliability. Moreover, retraining models for each operating context imposes significant constraints due to high data requirements, computational resources, and time. Considering this, we propose a novel context-aware multimodal late fusion approach that integrates a lightweight gating network within our probabilistic calibration framework. The gating network extracts environmental context and dynamically modulates the detection outputs of pre-trained object detectors based on the inferred context, without retraining of the detectors. Our methodology is evaluated on a modified KITTI dataset, in which the camera images and lidar pointclouds are augmented for varying fog levels. Experimental results show that our approach yields an approximately 14% relative improvement over non-adaptive late fusion baselines, achieving a consistent average precision of 56% across different fog levels.

While conventional camera-based surveillance systems and metal detectors can provide a sufficient level of security when used appropriately, they have fundamental limitations that reduce their applicability. Camera-based systems are unable to detect occluded or concealed threats and metal detectors require each person to enter through a narrow opening one at a time, leading to congestion issues and limited use in large crowds. A WiFi-based security system has the potential to be a complementary modality that is able to handle occlusions or concealment and is not hindered by strict spatial configurations. In this paper, we propose use Channel State Information estimated from WiFi-signals to detect concealed handguns. To this end we collect a dataset of aligned WiFi signals and RGB images that we call the WiFire dataset. We also propose a deep learning model called WiFireNet tailored to detect concealed handguns in WiFi signals using vision-based supervision signals. Our results show that concealed handgun detection is possible in WiFi and has promise as a complementary modality to surveillance cameras and metal detectors. We release the dataset, model and code to facilitate the further research into WiFi-based handgun detection.

Vision-language models (VLMs) that segment from language must pass the location of the referent to a pixel decoder. Probing a frozen segmentation VLM, we find that this attention yields 18 to 22 more gIoU than the [SEG] hidden state when read by the same probe, that it gains nothing from the image where the hidden state does, and that it is concentrated in the late layers. Code and models are available at https://eslambakr.github.io/attseg_project_page/

Emory Salaun, Syed Ayon, Kaleel Mahmood, Shaun Wallace
The rapid advancement of image-to-text extraction systems and large language models (LLMs) poses new challenges for educational assessment by making assignment materials easy to transcribe and solve with minimal human effort. To address this problem, we present AIRRI (Artificial Intelligence Resilient Reading Interface), a framework for generating machine-resistant educational content, a dataset of higher-education assignments for evaluation, and an initial evaluation of the human readability of AIRRI machine-resistant text designs. AIRRI employs two categories of machine-resistance techniques. First, AIRRI applies image transformations including character spacing, word spacing, line spacing, character opacity variation, stripe overlays, and image noise. Second, AIRRI applies decision-based adversarial attacks: RayS, SurFree, and ADBA. We evaluate AIRRI against three image-to-text systems: Tesseract, EasyOCR, and the transformer-based GOT-OCR2 model. Our results show that AIRRI substantially degrades automated text extraction performance. AIRRI increased character error rates for EasyOCR (6.9% to 55.9%), Tesseract (2.3% to 100.0%), and GOT-OCR2 (30.7% to 48.1%). Word error rates increased for EasyOCR (24.9% to 96.7%) and Tesseract (10.7% to 100.0%). Among the evaluated decision-based attacks, ADBA consistently produced the largest degradation in image-to-text performance, while RayS and SurFree produced more moderate reductions. EasyOCR and Tesseract were generally more susceptible to both image-based and adversarial perturbations than the transformer-based GOT-OCR2 model. Our findings suggest that AIRRI can significantly reduce the reliability of image-to-text-to-LLM workflows, increasing the effort required for AI-assisted assignment completion.

☆ UniW(A)M: A Unified Mixture-of-Experts Framework for World and World-Action Models ICLR
Jingbo Xu, Jianjie Fang, Zhuohang Li, Zihao Song, Zhaolu Wang, Xvyuan Liu, Xin Zhang, Haisheng Su, Yinzhou Tang, Chen Gao, Wei Wu, Yong Li
World models (WMs) and world-action models (WAMs) focus on future world prediction and executable action generation, respectively. Although these models learn shared physical dynamics and interaction semantics from embodied trajectories, they are typically trained in isolation, which restricts knowledge reuse between prediction and control. The central challenge is therefore to develop a unified learning framework that shares these dynamics while preserving the distinct modeling capabilities required by each paradigm. We propose UniW(A)M, a mixture-of-experts world-(action) model built upon diffusion Transformers that unifies action-conditioned world modeling and diverse WAM variants. Shared experts capture common dynamics, while atomic capability experts are reused across interfaces so that each interface keeps its own conditional pathway. At deployment, a plug-in adaptive interface router (PAIR) learns from a small subset of target-task chunk scenarios to select a suitable WAM interface for each execution chunk, balancing task success and execution efficiency while keeping the backbone frozen. We evaluate UniW(A)M on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and three real-world manipulation tasks, where it achieves 88.3% average real-world success versus 76.7% for the strongest baseline. On WorldArena, it leads action-conditioned world modeling on all three tasks. AC-WM co-training contributes to action generation on every action interface and PAIR raises OOD success from 63.3% to 76.7%.

☆ CryoTracer: A Synthetic-to-Real System for Filament Instance Tracing in Cryo-EM
Radosław Kuczbański, Wojciech Kozłowski, Mateusz Grzesiuk, Konrad Karanowski, Lukas Frey, Andrzej Rzepiela, Maciej Zięba
Particle picking in cryo-electron microscopy is commonly formulated as an object-detection problem in which individual particles are represented by bounding boxes, a natural representation for globular particles but a poor match for filaments that can extend across an entire micrograph. Existing methods reconstruct filament trajectories by linking local predictions in a separate post-processing stage, decoupling detection from instance formation and creating potential ambiguities at gaps and crossings. Directly preserving filament identity is particularly useful for polymorphic specimens, where segments originating from the same filament should remain associated. However, learning such instance-level representations is challenging because expert centerline annotations are scarce and costly to obtain. We introduce CryoTracer, a synthetic-to-real framework that addresses this limitation through procedural micrograph generation, transformer-based polyline prediction, and specimen-specific fine-tuning. Procedural pretraining exposes the model to diverse filament geometries, intersections, and imaging conditions before adaptation using a limited number of fully annotated experimental micrographs. CryoTracer represents filaments as ordered centerline polylines and optimizes their geometry using an orientation-invariant discrete Fréchet objective, enabling consistent learning regardless of tracing direction. Evaluation on established and newly expert-annotated datasets shows that CryoTracer improves instance-level filament recovery over existing particle-detection approaches. These results establish end-to-end polyline prediction as a practical alternative to detection-and-linking pipelines for recovering complete filament instances with limited micrograph annotation budgets. Code and data are available at https://github.com/cryotracer/cryotracer

Rong Li, Shijie Li, Jiangyong Huang, Lingdong Kong, Jiaming Zhou, Dongyue Lu, Zeying Gong, Baoxiong Jia, Junwei Liang, Siyuan Huang
Vision-language models (VLMs) struggle with metric and multi-view relationships that remain implicit in RGB observations. Geometry foundation models recover this structure from RGB, but existing methods either fuse the estimated features with visual tokens and learn to use them from question answering alone, or align VLM latents with geometry features. Capturing geometry, however, does not ensure its use: zeroing the aligned latents of a released feature-alignment model leaves its accuracy unchanged. We introduce GeoReader, a framework that learns geometric representations for the VLM that reads them. First, we train lightweight Geometric Readers to produce continuous input tokens, supervising them with geometry descriptions decoded by a frozen VLM, so that the Readers express geometry in a form the target model can already read. We then freeze the Readers to preserve this interface while fine-tuning the VLM on spatial QA, with geometry injection conditioned on the question. Geometry descriptions serve only as training targets: at inference, the VLM answers directly from the continuous geometric tokens without generating a geometry chain of thought. With geometry predicted from RGB images, our approach reaches 94.3 on MindCube-Tiny with Qwen3-VL-4B and, with a multi-source QA mixture, an average of 72.5 across six additional spatial benchmarks with Qwen3.5-9B. These results suggest that a useful geometric representation is one the receiving model can use, not merely one from which geometry can be reconstructed.

☆ Orientation Estimation of Cryo-EM Images for Molecules with Arbitrary Symmetry by Semidefinite Programming
Yunpeng Shi, Amit Singer, Jinxin Wang, Ruiyi Yang
This paper extends the non-unique games framework introduced in Bandeira et al. (2020) to address symmetric structures. Precisely, we consider the problem \[ \begin{aligned} \underset{g_1,\ldots,g_n\in \mathcal{G}}{\operatorname{min}}\,\, \frac{1}{|S|}\sum_{i,j=1}^n \sum_{s\in S} f_{ij}(g_i s g_j^{-1}), \end{aligned} \] where $\mathcal{G}$ is a compact group, $S\subset \mathcal{G}$ is a finite subgroup of symmetry elements, and $f_{ij}:\mathcal{G}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is a loss function. A notable example is common lines based orientation estimation of cryo-EM images for molecules with point group symmetry $S$, where $\mathcal{G}$ is the rotation group $\operatorname{SO}(3)$. With a semidefinite programming relaxation, we turn the problem into a convex program that is solved with the alternating direction method of multipliers. Unlike existing approaches which are tailored to specific symmetry groups, ours provides a unified computational framework for addressing all point group symmetries. We demonstrate the applicability of the proposed algorithm on the cryo-EM orientation estimation problem on both simulated and experimental datasets. In particular, our algorithm is effective in generating high-quality ab initio models from only a few class averages computed from experimental images.
☆ Just Respect the Semantics: Image-Token Compression via Pre-LLM Semantic Variable-Resolution Tokenization and In-LLM Relevance Pruning
Tianhao Fu, Austin Wang, Charles Chen, Roby Aldave-Garza, Victor Xie, Xiyue Jiao, Yucheng Chen, Martin Tin
Image-token compression must reduce computation without hurting the semantics. We introduce Varest, guided by semantic fungibility: tokens within a coherent semantic region can be summarized coarsely, while object boundaries and literal text require finer distinctions. Object and text localizers guide variable-resolution merging, preserving spatial coverage and finer detail at boundaries and text. Learned [REL] registers then prune visual tokens after early decoder processing. Training across budgets enables one checkpoint per backbone. Across three backbones and 13 benchmarks, Varest outperforms 15 baselines in mean performance retention at every evaluated budget, retaining 86.10-92.33% of full-token performance with only 5.56% of the original layer-averaged image-token count.

Yidi Liu, Haozhe Wang, Jie Xiao, Kai Zhu, Xueyang Fu, Zheng-Jun Zha
Agentic visual generation produces experience that can improve the native understanding (agent) and generation roles of a unified multimodal backbone, but task success alone does not determine which role should learn. Generator updates can also make the agent's action supervision stale. We introduce RSIgen, a task-centric reciprocal self-improvement framework linking learning allocation, supervision refresh, and recursive curriculum construction. Dynamic Responsibility Routing (DRR) uses matched interventions on evidence, inputs, and supported actions to select learning recipients and construct compatible training targets. After generator learning, RSIgen re-evaluates the relative utility of tested actions with branch inputs held fixed to refresh agent supervision; the retained roles then construct the next curriculum. Across BAGEL, Qwen-Image, and Wan-Image-7B, RSIgen improves AgentGen-Bench Full Overall9 by 3.2--3.3 points over a three-cycle SearchGen adaptation with action costs. Wan controls support allocation gains at matched role-level training exposure, refresh gains at a matched adaptation budget, and benefits from updated curriculum sources while recipients continue learning. In blind evaluation on 200 real-user requests, pooled tie-adjusted preference scores against the same baseline reach 70.0% for task completion and 64.9% for visual quality.

Reliable robot autonomy requires reasoning about the world from partial and noisy observations. However, many perception systems model only visible scene regions, rely on fixed semantic categories, and assume reliable sensor measurements. These assumptions break under occlusion, novel object encounters, and sensor degradation. In this paper, I present a research vision for incompleteness-aware scene understanding. I organize this vision around three fundamental challenges: incomplete evidence, incomplete knowledge, and incomplete sensor reliability. I discuss my research contributions toward addressing these challenges through amodal perception, semantic occupancy forecasting, open-world scene understanding, label-efficient learning, and uncertainty-guided multi-modal fusion. Building on these contributions, I outline future research directions toward belief-centric 4D scene representations. These representations aim to jointly model geometry, semantics, motion, and uncertainty. I also discuss active sensing and safe adaptation strategies that allow robots to reduce uncertainty through interaction. The goal is to develop calibrated and actionable scene representations that support reliable autonomy in dynamic, open-world environments.

☆ PlanPath: Exploration-Guided Orchestration for Patient-Level Pathology Reasoning
Jiusong Ge, Mingzhao He, Qidong Liu, Chunbao Wang, Chunze Yang, Di Zhang, Jiashuai Liu, Mireia Crispin-Ortuzar, Huazhu Fu, Chen Li, Zeyu Gao
A patient's pathology case spans tens of slides from distinct specimens and anatomical sites, each carrying non-redundant, site-specific evidence. Forming a patient-level conclusion therefore requires locating the slides relevant to a given question and integrating complementary findings across them. However, existing pathology agents analyze one slide at a time and describe morphology rather than measure it, leaving evidence acquisition across a patient's specimens and patient-level quantification underexplored. To address this gap, we propose PlanPath, an agentic framework for patient-level pathology visual question answering (VQA). PlanPath turns the question into an exploration plan that specifies the evidence required, routes to the slides likely to carry it, and drives coarse-to-fine acquisition from tissue architecture down to individual cells. Tissue- and cell-level tools supply the counts, proportions, and extents, which PlanPath aggregates across slides into a traceable answer. To enable evaluation, we build two patient-level VQA datasets for renal and gastric cancer, averaging 15 WSIs per patient, with pathologist-verified question-answer pairs derived from diagnostic reports. Experimental results show that PlanPath outperforms the strongest baseline by 9.4% and 12.1% in overall accuracy on the two datasets and further improves existing slide-level agents when plugged into our framework. The dataset and code are available at: https://github.com/JSGe-AI/PlanPath_1.
☆ Texture Interpolation as Texton Matching ATC
Ido Madar, Gal Oren, Shai Avidan
Texture interpolation asks what should lie between two textures. Standard methods typically blend pixels or features at corresponding spatial locations, implicitly assuming that co-located elements should be mixed. For unrelated textures, however, this correspondence is arbitrary: a crack at one location has no particular relationship to a fiber at the same location in another image. We study whether this hidden pairing choice is itself a major determinant of interpolation quality. We represent textures as collections of local appearance vectors, or textons, and replace positional pairing with appearance-aware matching while keeping the encoder, representation, and decoder fixed. This isolates the effect of correspondence from changes in model capacity or training. Across texture pairs, appearance-aware matching consistently improves the distributional quality of interpolated midpoints over positional feature blending. Soft matching produces the strongest midpoint statistics, whereas one-to-one assignments yield more balanced transitions and closer agreement with the target endpoint. The same intervention also improves a second pretrained texture interpolator without retraining. These results identify correspondence as a first-class design choice in texture interpolation: meaningful transitions depend not only on how strongly two textures are mixed, but also on which local appearances are mixed with one another.

Augusta van Haren, Hanna Hoogen, Luca Pattavina, Quincy Rommen

PredRNN and its successor PredRNN-V2 address this challenge with spatiotemporal Long Short-Term Memory (ST-LSTM) units that maintain two separate memory states, at the cost of a relatively complex recurrent building block. In this work, we investigate whether the simpler gating of Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) can be transferred to spatiotemporal predictive learning. To this end, we develop a spatiotemporal GRU (ST-GRU) unit as a GRU-based alternative to the ST-LSTM. The ST-GRU replaces the ST-LSTM's three gates per memory state with two GRU-style gates (update and reset), and merges the temporal memory state into the hidden state, which reduces the number of parameters by about 5%. We incorporate the ST-GRU into PredRNN-V2 and evaluate the resulting model on the Moving MNIST video prediction benchmark, following the original experimental protocol. Averaged over ten predicted frames, the ST-GRU-based PredRNN-V2 achieves an MSE of 55.1, an SSIM of 0.883, an LPIPS of 0.065 and a PSNR of 19.53dB. It does not surpass the original ST-LSTM-based PredRNN-V2 on MSE, SSIM or PSNR, but it achieves a lower LPIPS and performs on par with the earlier ST-LSTM-based PredRNN, while using a simpler recurrent cell. These results suggest that ST-GRUs are a promising building block for spatiotemporal predictive learning and motivate further work on their design and integration.

A robot's world model must remember objects that leave the camera's view. FloWM, a learned world model, keeps them in a spatial grid of features that it moves with five built-in velocities. A node memory instead keeps each object's position and velocity as numbers. We compare them in FloWM's own block world, with an oracle-fed Kalman tracker as the node memory. How the grid is read changes its score: a single-cell probe finds 66% of out-of-view blocks, while FloWM's own probe 89%. FloWM also scores 8 points higher in view although no frame is shown, which we attribute to its write-back of its own predictions. Out of view, the tracker reaches FloWM's range in 14KB against 5.6MB, with no probe. On diagonal motion, outside its five velocities, FloWM finds 11% of blocks even after fine-tuning, while the unchanged tracker keeps 93%. Faster blocks defeat both until one more allowed speed takes the tracker to 94%, where FloWM's built-in shifts would need 25 copies of its grid. A learned node memory must still replace the oracles and handle velocity under noise, long gaps, and the bounce.

Carmen Oliver Huidobro, Mikolaj Czerkawski, Kevin Monsalvez-Pozo, Cesar Aybar, Gustau Camps-Valls, Oscar J. Pellicer-Valero

Existing preference poisoning attacks either corrupt explicit supervision signals or require visible triggers, making them detectable under human inspection. Causal attention, however, lets the hidden states of a part observe only the parts that precede it. To force this compact bottleneck to retain sufficient scene information, a query-based Gaussian decoder uses scene-independent queries to attend to the learned tokens and recover an explicit, renderable set of 3D Gaussian primitives. We trace these failures to two limitations of the prevailing paradigm of retaining the highest-ranked native patches. A single importance ranking overlooks the complementary evidence required by different tasks, while sparse patch selection disrupts both image content and spatial integrity. To address these limitations, we propose Bifocal, a training-free, two-stage pruning method built on a mixed-granularity framework. It allocates separate budgets to query-focused and image-intrinsic evidence, complemented by a pooled coarse representation of the entire image. Before the LLM, Bifocal matches question words to visual regions through a soft conjunction balanced against norm-debiased image saliency, while selecting image-intrinsic evidence to maximize representational coverage. Inside the LLM, it further prunes tokens using density-adjusted text-to-image attention. With roughly a quarter of the original visual tokens, Bifocal is the only evaluated method to retain over 90% of unpruned performance in every ability group across all three models, and ranks first on average in all nine model-budget settings. The code is available at: https://github.com/EIT-NLP/Bifocal

Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have shown strong potential for remote sensing understanding, yet reliable reasoning remains challenging when tasks require fine-grained visual grounding and multi-step inference. Existing approaches typically rely on either costly pre-constructed reasoning trajectories or self-generated signals such as response consistency, which can reinforce shared errors and provide unreliable supervision. We introduce \textbf{Reasoning--Diagnosis Self-Evolution (ReDiS)}, a framework that separates reasoning exploration from candidate evaluation while allowing the two processes to evolve jointly. ReDiS instantiates two role-specific experts from a shared multimodal backbone: a \textbf{Reasoner} that explores diverse visual evidence--answer candidates and a \textbf{Diagnoser} that jointly evaluates the complete candidate set and provides credibility-aware feedback. As the Reasoner evolves, it exposes new candidate distributions and failure modes; the Diagnoser adapts to these changes and, in turn, reshapes the learning signal for subsequent exploration. To handle groups in which all sampled answers are incorrect and group-relative advantages vanish, we further introduce \textbf{Failure-Triggered Recovery (FTR)}, which provides minimal outcome-level correction without prescribing intermediate reasoning trajectories. Experiments on LHRS-Bench, MME-RS, and CHOICE show consistent improvements over Qwen3.5 backbones at 0.8B, 2B, and 4B scales. ReDiS improves category-averaged accuracy by 6.47 percentage points at 0.8B, while ReDiS-4B achieves the highest average performance among the compared remote sensing MLLMs.

With the rapid development of deep learning, supervised convolutional neural network methods have greatly improved the performance of low-dose computed tomography (CT) denoising. However, they require paired noisy-clean training data, which is difficult to obtain in practice. Some classic self-supervised denoising methods rely on the assumption of pixel-wise independent noise, making them ineffective for correlated noise in low-dose CT (LDCT) images. Considering the high similarity and weaker noise correlation between adjacent CT slices, several recently proposed self-supervised methods use adjacent LDCT slices for training. Nevertheless, these approaches fail to effectively account for the non-rigid misalignment between slices caused by anatomical variation, hindering them from satisfying the equal-mean condition required by the classic Noise2Noise framework. In this paper, we propose Noise2Match, a self-supervised LDCT denoising method based on adaptive inter-slice matching. Noise2Match introduces an inter-slice matching network to model the label transition process between adjacent slices, and then applies correction to the denoiser's outputs to better satisfy the equal-mean condition. We theoretically prove that, under idealized conditions, training Noise2Match using adjacent LDCT slices is equivalent to supervised training with paired noisy-clean images. We further find that Noise2Match can also effectively perform low-dose conebeam CT (CBCT) denoising, which could be attributed to its correction operation that reduces inter-slice noise correlation. To the best of our knowledge, Noise2Match is the first effective image-domain self-supervised method for low-dose CBCT. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Noise2Match outperforms existing image-domain selfsupervised methods, offering broader applicability and higher practical value.

This challenge is amplified in the RGB-only setting, where pose cues, category-level commonality, and instance-specific variation are entangled in appearance without direct geometric constraints, making it difficult for existing frameworks to learn a representation that is truly aligned with the category-level estimation objective. To address this problem, we propose SchemaPose, a schema-guided framework for RGB-based category-level pose estimation. SchemaPose equips the estimation pipeline with an explicit parametric schema for modeling category-level regularities together with structured instance variation, and uses the inferred schema variables to guide pose-related prediction in an end-to-end query-based framework. The same formulation also supports template instantiation, synthetic annotation, and pose learning within a unified framework. Experiments on synthetic and real data show that SchemaPose achieves state-of-the-art performance among RGB-based methods for category-level 9D pose estimation.

☆ Hallucination-aware Faithful Reasoning in Remote Sensing
Yi Liu, Jing Zhang, Xiang Feng, Xiaoyu Tian, Haonan Guo, Di Wang, Zengmao Wang, Bo Du
Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated promising capabilities for remote sensing reasoning, yet they frequently generate visually unsupported reasoning that contradicts the visual evidence. Existing post-training methods optimize primarily for final-answer correctness, providing limited supervision for identifying and correcting hallucinations that arise during the reasoning process. To address this limitation, we propose \textbf{FaithRS}, a hallucination-aware self-reflection framework for faithful reasoning in remote sensing. We first construct \textbf{SFHD-43K}, a dataset of 43K structured, fine-grained hallucination annotations, and train a detector to identify hallucination types, underlying causes, and supporting visual evidence. FaithRS then incorporates this diagnostic feedback into a Safe Detector-Guided Corrective Rollout framework, where a safety-aware gate selectively determines whether and how to revise the response. Training is driven by a composite reward that jointly optimizes answer accuracy, reasoning faithfulness, hallucination reduction, format compliance, and revision safety. Experiments with Qwen3.5 backbones (0.8B, 4B, and 9B) show consistent improvements across four remote sensing benchmarks, with gains of up to 11.64 points.
☆ Visual Sevoing from Lines
Nicolas Andreff, Bernard Espiau, Radu Horaud
In this work, we present a fundamentally new approach to visual servoing using lines. It is based on a theoretical and geometrical study of the main line representations which allowed us to define a new representation, the so-called binormalized Plucker coordinates. They are particularly well suited to visual servoing. Indeed, they allow the definition of a proper image line alignment concept. The control law which realizes such an alignment has moreover several properties: partial decoupling between rotation and translation, analytical inversion of the motion equations and global asymptotic stability conditions. This control law was validated both in simulation and experimentally in the specific case of an orthogonal trihedron.

City-scale 3D grounding is commonly formulated as candidate ranking, which requires precomputed instance proposals and becomes inefficient in large outdoor scenes. We propose Urbex, an agentic vision-language framework that instead casts grounding as active spatial search. Urbex represents a city-scale 3D scene as an interactive multi-view environment, allowing a VLM agent to query landmarks, zoom into local regions, render oblique views, and commit a grounded bounding box. We optimize this tool-use policy with reinforcement learning on CityRefer, using smooth localization rewards and lightweight shaping rewards for efficient exploration. Experiments show that Urbex achieves the best Hit@1 and IoU on CityRefer, supports candidate-free grounding without ground-truth boxes, and is substantially faster than the strongest city-scale ranking baseline. Zero-shot results on STPLS3D-Refer further indicate improved cross-scene robustness.

Urban spatial intelligence calls for 3D cities that agents can measure, interpret, and modify across successive tasks. Maintaining such cities as persistent, code-based states requires lightweight acquisition and support for consistent state updates without repeated dense reconstruction. We further develop Air2Code to construct this representation by combining visual structure extraction with adapted metric depth estimation. To address occlusion and incomplete coverage, recovered structure and observed appearance guide generative completion and subsequent structure-aware 3D generation for buildings and backgrounds. Experiments on CitySample-Aerial and UrbanScene3D demonstrate substantially more accurate metric structure recovery and superior visual fidelity to the target cities compared with the evaluated baselines. Across 50 task chains of 50 steps each, CityCode supports continued querying, editing, planning, and historical restoration over evolving city states. Together, CityCode and Air2Code turn sparse aerial observations into persistent, agent-operable urban worlds for long-horizon urban spatial intelligence.

☆ ShoeFit: A New Dataset and Dual-image-stream DiT Framework for Virtual Footwear Try-On NeurIPS

Virtual footwear try-on (VFTON), a critical yet underexplored area in virtual try-on (VTON), aims to synthesize faithful try-on results given diverse footwear and model images while maintaining 3D consistency and texture authenticity. Unlike conventional garment-focused VTON methods, VFTON presents unique challenges due to (1) Data Scarcity, which arises from the difficulty of perfectly matching product shoes with models wearing the identical ones, (2) Viewpoint Misalignment, where the target foot pose and source shoe views are always misaligned, leading to incomplete texture information and detail distortion, and (3) Background-induced Color Distortion, where complex material of footwear interacts with environmental lighting, causing unintended color contamination. To address these challenges, we introduce MVShoes, a multi-view shoe try-on dataset consisting of 7305 well-annotated image triplets, covering diverse footwear categories and challenging try-on scenarios. Furthermore, we propose a dual-stream DiT architecture, ShoeFit, designed to mitigate viewpoint misalignment through Multi-View Conditioning with 3D Rotary Position Embedding, and alleviate background-induced distortion using the LayeredRefAttention which leverages background features to modulate footwear latents. The proposed framework effectively decouples shoe appearance from environmental interferences while preserving high-quality texture detail through decoupled denoising and conditioning branches. Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate that our method substantially improves rendering fidelity and robustness under challenging real-world product shoes, establishing a new benchmark in high-fidelity footwear try-on synthesis.

☆ Omni-RS: Unifying Multi-Task Understanding and Generation in Remote Sensing

Practical remote sensing applications often require both understanding and generation capabilities for the same geographic scene. To bridge this gap, we propose Omni-RS, a unified framework supporting four remote sensing understanding tasks and five generation tasks. Specifically, we introduce the "Scene-Guided Two-Stage Training" strategy, which first adapts a multimodal large language model to remote sensing understanding and then uses its hidden states to guide a diffusion transformer for image generation. To enable joint learning across diverse generation tasks, we construct UniGen, a unified multi-task generation dataset, by organizing heterogeneous remote sensing data into a unified format. Furthermore, we introduce "Detailed Visual Conditioning", which uses visual conditions encoded by a VAE to guide the generation process, thereby supporting additional generation tasks that require reference images. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Omni-RS performs exceptionally well in understanding tasks and has achieved outstanding results in a variety of generative tasks.
☆ AffectWorld: Benchmarking Emotion-Driven Future World Prediction
Changhao Song, Yacong Chen, Hui Gao, Yazhou Zhang, Peng Zhang
The world encompasses both physical environments and human actors. Predicting its evolution requires understanding both physical laws and how emotions shape human actions. However, existing world model benchmarks primarily assess physical plausibility and perceptual quality, leaving emotion-driven world evolution largely untested.We introduce AffectWorld, a benchmark that evaluates the chain Emotion-Action-World State through three tasks: World-State Consistency, Emotion-Action Consistency, and Causal Consistency. It comprises 1,498 everyday video samples annotated with plausible emotions, action tendencies, and atomic world-state constraints. A counterfactual subset of 233 samples tests whether changing an agent's emotion under fixed scene and event conditions yields corresponding changes in actions and consequences. We define eight metrics across the three tasks and an additional counterfactual metric, combining automatic visual assessment with human-calibrated VLM/LLM judgments. Evaluations of five SoTA world models (e.g., Cosmos3) required world-state change scores of 0.100-0.280 and counterfactual emotion sensitivity scores of 0.027-0.070 on a [0, 1] scale. These results reveal substantial gaps in generating the consequences of emotion-driven actions and adapting future predictions to emotional interventions. AffectWorld provides a testbed for advancing world models that capture how emotions shape future physical and social states.

Detectors of logical anomalies, such as missing, extra or wrongly combined parts, usually score a test image by its distance from normal (good) images. They achieve near-perfect image-level AUROC on standard industrial anomaly detection benchmarks such as MVTec LOCO, but their robustness to changes in capture conditions remains largely unexamined. Under a heterogeneous perturbation protocol in which each test image is randomly kept unaltered or subjected to a brightness reduction or a zoom-out transformation, the normal-reference methods we tested lose 9.7 to 34.1 AUROC points, and two of the strongest, CSAD and SALAD, fall from 97.7% and 96.4% to 68.1% and 62.3%. From a short description of each product, a language model derives anomaly types and editing instructions, an image editor applies them to normal images, and the classifier learns to separate the edited images from automatically discovered normal sub-modes. With its full training recipe, the framework reaches 94.9% AUROC on clean images, 1.5 to 2.8 points below SALAD and CSAD, and 94.1% under the perturbation protocol. Trained without brightness or zoom-out augmentation, so that neither test perturbation occurs in training, it still reaches 92.5% (93.2% clean). These results suggest that clean benchmark scores can hide a strong sensitivity to capture conditions, and that learning the decision from both normal images and rule violations may reduce it.

☆ LongForcing: Scaling Temporal Manifold Matching for Long-Horizon World Rollout
Ziyu Zhu, Zhaoxu Sun, Fan Jiang, Mengchao Wang, Junfeng Ni, Ting-Bing Xu, Zhicheng Liu, Mu Xu
Autoregressive video diffusion models have emerged as a foundation for long-horizon world rollout. However, when extended far beyond their training windows, these models suffer from progressive drift: visual quality deteriorates, motion becomes inconsistent, and object identity gradually collapses as generated frames are recursively reused as context. We study a supervision-horizon gap: short-horizon distillation leaves later rollout states without direct supervision. We show that matching short-window marginals need not determine long-horizon behavior, while longer on-policy trajectories expose delayed failures to training. This motivates temporal manifold matching at scale for long-horizon world models. Building on this insight, we introduce LongForcing, a distillation approach that scales teacher supervision to long student self-rollouts. LongForcing preserves the short-horizon teacher-forcing and causal ODE-distillation stages, while replacing the realscore teacher in the final distribution-matching stage with an extended-horizon bidirectional teacher. The long-horizon teacher supervises extended student self-rollouts using the standard distribution-matching formulation, without modifying the student architecture or increasing inference cost. We evaluate LongForcing on text-to-video generation and interactive action-conditioned world models, achieving a VBench Quality score of 85.52 and improving WorldRoamBench 60s action score by 23.9 points in first-person ablations. Qualitative stress tests further sample interactive rollouts up to 24 hours, far beyond the training horizon. These results suggest that scaling supervision along the temporal axis is a practical step toward long-horizon world models. The project website and code are at https://github.com/Fantasy-AMAP/LongForcing.

Then, we have discussed them in terms of the critical situations that they claim to handle. Furthermore, we present the available resources, datasets and libraries. Then, we conclude with several promising directions for future research. For the sake of reading, this survey is divided into two parts: 1) "Traditional and Recent Approaches for Infrared Small Target Detection : Overview, Challenges and Perspectives (Part 1)" about conventional and low-rank and sparse decomposition (model-based methods), and 2) "Traditional and Recent Approaches for Infrared Small Target Detection : Overview, Challenges and Perspectives (Part 2)" about deep learning models (data-based methods).

The cleaner domain-specificity contrast, separate learned source scales without their variance penalty versus one shared learned source scale, is -0.13 pp (95% CI [-0.53, 0.27]). Its 90% CI lies within a revision-stage $\pm 1$ pp smallest effect of practical interest (TOST p = .003), supporting equivalence only for the source-selected suite macro, not every dataset, target, or final-step endpoint. The study thus supplies a bounded negative result for this scalar training package; it does not test or refute genuine hyperbolic representation learning.

Human evaluation, natural-caption controls, prompt-enhancement experiments, diversity analyses, and transfer to LTX-2.3 further support the robustness and transferability of these gains, while VARI requires no additional inference-time module.

Oriol Rabasseda, Zenjie Li, Kamal Nasrollahi, Sergio Escalera
Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated strong zero-shot reasoning across diverse domains, but their potential for Human-Object Interaction (HOI) remains unexplored. Unlike traditional HOI approaches that rely on extensive labeled datasets and fixed interaction taxonomies, MLLMs offer flexible reasoning, making them well-suited for dynamic, real-world scenarios. In this work, we present the first systematic study of MLLMs for HOI recognition and detection within a pipeline that combines an external object detector for entity localization with zero-shot multimodal reasoning for interaction understanding. We introduce a benchmark framework for principled zero-shot evaluation, consisting of (i) a unified taxonomy of zero-shot prompting strategies, and (ii) a methodology that transforms token-level logits into interaction scores, enabling fair comparison with specialized HOI models under standard metrics. To support prompt-based evaluation, we additionally construct new question-answer annotations for standard HOI datasets, transforming them into a format suitable for MLLMs. Building on this, we propose two visual prompting strategies, namely Objects as Context and Black Other Objects, that guide MLLMs to target objects while preserving scene context. Experiments on HICO, HICO-DET, and V-COCO demonstrate state-of-the-art zero-shot performance, achieving 53.50 mAP on HICO and 23.69 mAP on HICO-DET. Overall, our work provides a principled benchmarking framework for MLLMs in HOI, opening the door to new models and datasets and enabling flexible open-world interaction understanding.
☆ FlowCred: Hierarchical Credit Assignment and Functional Coordination for Joint Text-to-Video Post-Training
Mingxuan Zhu, Yanwei Huang, Shiyuan Liu, Xinzhi Zhang, Shujie Li, Yuanxing Zhang, Lu Chen
Prompt optimization and generator post-training are two complementary ways to improve text-to-video (T2V) generation, and recent systems increasingly train both modules jointly. However, optimizing a prompt policy and a video generator from the same terminal reward creates two ambiguities: prompt quality is confounded with stochastic generation, and the two modules may realize overlapping local improvements. We introduce FlowCred, a two-level framework for joint T2V post-training. First, hierarchical credit assignment uses matched prompt-seed rollout grids to separate prompt-level credit from prompt-conditioned generator residuals under shared randomness. Second, functional coordination probes alternative current-policy prompts at states from actual generation trajectories, providing generator-aware evidence for prompt optimization while selectively attenuating generator updates already supported by conditioning changes. Across multiple T2V benchmarks, FlowCred consistently improves matched joint-training baselines. On LTX-2.5, FlowCred improves a strictly matched joint-training control from 61.47 to 64.46 on T2V-CompBench and from 55.58 to 58.08 on StoryEval, without increasing decoded-video or reward-model-call budgets. Factorial and realized-update analyses show complementary contributions from prompt shaping and generator routing, while human evaluation and transfer across backbones and updater families provide further supporting evidence.
☆ Human-Inspired Asymmetric Collaboration for Dual-Student Semi-Supervised Medical Image Segmentation
Huiyi Ren, Ziming Fang, Jiaming Cai, Rui Xu, Haojie Li
Dual-student learning enriches predictive diversity in SSMIS by introducing a strongly augmented view alongside a weakly augmented view. Insufficient strong augmentation may homogenize the students, whereas excessive augmentation can corrupt anatomical evidence and destabilize collaboration. This challenge echoes feedback-regulated human instruction, where learners receive differentiated tasks and the task difficulty is continually adjusted according to their evolving responses. Inspired by these, we propose Human-Inspired Asymmetric Collaboration (HAC), a closed-loop dual-student framework that maintains weak--strong learning through adaptive difficulty calibration and geometry preservation. Specifically, Reinforcement-guided Difficulty Calibration (RDC) formulates strong-augmentation control as a window-level reinforcement learning process, using augmentation history, realized perturbations, and training responses to dynamically adjust the augmentation magnitude, operation number, and magnitude range. Meanwhile, the Gramian Geometry Preservation Constraint (G2PC) preserves the early-stage three-branch geometry through global volume and pairwise area constraints, preventing shared supervision from homogenizing the two students. Comprehensive evaluations across LA, Pancreas, and BraTS-2019 validate both the segmentation effectiveness and capability-aware difficulty calibration of HAC.
☆ H-DDCM: Hadamard Codebooks for Fast Generative Image and Video Compression
Or Ronai, Vladimir Kulikov, Tomer Michaeli
Training-free diffusion-based compression methods repurpose the generative priors of a diffusion or a flow model to compress data without retraining them as task-specific codecs. Recent codebook-based approaches such as Turbo-DDCM achieve strong perceptual quality at ultra-low bitrates, but their reliance on dense Gaussian codebooks remains costly in both memory and computation, and scales poorly with the large latent dimensions of modern image and video generators. Their combinatorial bitstream encoding further becomes computationally heavy at this scale. We introduce H-DDCM, a scalable generative compression framework that replaces Gaussian codebooks with implicit randomized Hadamard dictionaries. The fast Walsh-Hadamard transform allows for implicitly synthesizing full-dimensional dictionaries with $O(d \log d)$ compute for projection and reconstruction and $O(d)$ memory, without materializing the full-dimensional dictionary. We further introduce an efficient table-free lexicographic coding scheme that makes combinatorial encoding practical at larger dimensions. Beyond images, we adapt the framework to an autoregressive video flow model and develop a streaming compression scheme that periodically re-encodes recently reconstructed frames into a fresh KV-cache prefix, preserving temporal context across segments at no additional transmitted bits. This enables long-form, close to real-time generative video compression on a single GPU. Across image and video benchmarks, H-DDCM achieves competitive rate-distortion-perception performance while substantially reducing the memory and computational overhead of codebook-based training-free generative compression.
comment: Project's webpage at https://h-ddcm.github.io/
☆ SYNPRED: A Synergistic Approach to Multimodal Learning for Clinical Prediction
Ivana Janíčková, Yen Y. Tan, Thomas H. Helbich, Philipp Seeböck, Julieta Di Marco, Zsuzsanna Bago-Horvath, Ulrike Heber, Thomas Spiegel, Georg Langs
Multimodal medical data captures complementary aspects of disease. It provides a comprehensive basis for diagnosis and the identification of biological associations linked to progression or treatment response. Established contrastive learning approaches exploit shared information across modalities, but fall short in exploiting complementary, modality-specific signals relevant for a task. Here, we propose a synergistic multimodal variational autoencoder (VAE) framework that separates task-relevant unimodal and multimodal information from instance-specific variation task-irrelevant, allowing complementary signals across modalities to be leveraged for prediction. The method yields benefits even if modalities are missing at test time. We evaluate the method on a treatment response prediction task using medical imaging and RNA data. Empirical comparison with alignment-based and multimodal VAE state-of-the-art approaches demonstrates improved multimodal prediction performance, and consistent benefits for prediction from a single modality after multimodal training. The full code can be found here: https://github.com/cirmuw/SYNPRED.
☆ APT: Feedback-Driven Agentic Post-Training for Text-to-Image Generation
Sirui Zhang, Fangyun Wei, Dong Chen, Jinjing Zhao, Yitong Wang, Yunuo Chen, Baining Guo, Zheng-Jun Zha
Post-training is crucial for improving text-to-image models, yet existing pipelines typically rely on manually curated training data and fixed training distributions. We introduce APT (Agentic Post-Training), a fully automated framework that adaptively post-trains a base model according to its evolving capability profile. APT coordinates three agents to construct evaluation sets from user requirements, diagnose model-specific strengths and failure modes, and generate reinforcement learning data with an adaptive prompt distribution that emphasizes underperforming capabilities. By repeatedly evaluating, diagnosing, and updating the generator, APT lets the current model's behavior shape its next training tasks, forming a feedback loop inspired by recursive self-improvement. For general-purpose settings without user-specified evaluation scenarios, we further develop an evaluation harness that enables broad and diverse evaluation set generation. Experiments across multiple base models, benchmarks, and generation architectures demonstrate that APT is model-agnostic, benchmark-agnostic, architecture-agnostic, and fully automated.
☆ LensErase: A Foundation Model for Erase Anything
Yunuo Chen, Xiuyu Wu, Qinhong Yang, Jinjing Zhao, Yanchen Dong, Sirui Zhang, Dong Chen, Fangyun Wei, Lei Shi, Ji Li, Dongdong Chen, Guo Lu, Yan Lu, Baining Guo
We introduce LensErase, a general-purpose mask-based Erase Anything foundation model designed to cover a broad spectrum of real-world erase scenarios. LensErase supports diverse objects, visual text, watermarks, associated visual effects, multiple-object removal, and a wide range of object scales, aspect ratios, and image resolutions. First, to enable such broad coverage, we construct LensErase-100M, a large-scale dataset containing 101.07 million paired source-mask-target examples spanning diverse erase scenarios. Second, we pretrain LensErase from the text-to-image model Lens, adapting its strong generative prior to mask-based erasing. To efficiently incorporate the source image and erase mask, we propose Mask-Aware RoPE, a 3D rotary positional encoding that directly injects mask information into the source-image tokens without introducing a separate mask token sequence. Finally, we refine the model through supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning with contract-guided, region-aware rewards, and apply TraceFusion at inference to preserve high-fidelity content outside the effective edit region. Across six public benchmarks and the proposed LensErase-Bench, LensErase achieves substantial improvements under both reference-based objective metrics and reference-free VLM evaluation. We hope LensErase can serve as a foundational model for erase-related applications and systems.

☆ Scaling Vision Transformers Without Training: Prune-and-Merge Token Compression NeurIPS
Vatsal, Soumil Malhotra, Priyanshu Chahal, Sanjeev Kumar
Vision Transformers achieve strong performance but incur high computational costs from quadratic token interactions. Training-free token reduction methods improve efficiency, but their robustness remains underexplored. We propose Prune-and Merge ViT, a training-free framework for off-the-shelf models. It combines class attention-based pruning with similarity-based merging to reduce redundancy while preserving semantic information. To evaluate robustness we introduce two metrics. Relative Accuracy Drop (RAD) measures relative accuracy degradation under transformations, and Prediction Flip Rate (PFR) quantifies prediction consistency. On pretrained ViT and DeiT, Prune-and-Merge reduces computation competitively while maintaining robustness and better accuracy than existing token reduction methods. Our analysis suggests that hybrid token reduction does not introduce hallucination-like behavior and preserves prediction stability for common image transformations.
comment: Accepted at the GlobalSouthAI Workshop at NeurIPS 2026; 12 pages
☆ Data-Free Continual Learning for World Action Model with Rectified Generative Replay
Kaipeng Fang, Hangxu Liu, Chaojian Shi, Yunsong Zhou, Hongzi Zhu, Minyi Guo, Jingkuan Song, Lianli Gao
World action models (WAMs) built on pretrained video generation models adapt quickly to new robotic tasks, but they forget previously learned tasks under sequential fine-tuning. Experience replay (ER) mitigates such forgetting by rehearsing data of previous tasks, yet this data is often unavailable in robotics, where a policy is deployed as weights only and its training data is not shared along with it. In this work, we ask whether a WAM can achieve data-free continual learning by regenerating its own past. Our key observation is that a WAM can indeed autoregressively regenerate complete rollouts of previously learned tasks and replay them to mitigate forgetting. However, replaying such raw rollouts still lags far behind replaying real data, which we attribute to two issues. First, the WAM is unable to recognize task completion and keeps generating purposeless motion after the task is done. Second, under open-loop generation, the generated actions gradually drift away from the generated observations. To address both issues, we present rectified generative replay (R$^2$-WAM), which truncates generated rollouts at task completion with an agentic evaluator and filters out rollouts whose actions are physically inconsistent with the observations. On the four LIBERO suites and five real-world tasks, R$^2$-WAM reduces forgetting by over 90% relative to sequential fine-tuning and nearly matches ER without accessing any data from previous tasks. Our analysis further reveals that forgetting in WAMs concentrates in inverse dynamics modeling: a forgotten WAM still produces visually plausible observations of previous tasks while its generated actions fail.
☆ COMPASS: Contextual Moment Prior Alignment for Generalizable AIGI Detection
Zhan Yang, Tiancheng Shen, Weijie Lyu, Shuo Chen, Bernard Ghanem, Yibo Yang, Ming-Hsuan Yang
Generalizable AI-generated image (AIGI) and deepfake detection remain challenging due to the asymmetry phenomenon, where adaptation to limited training distributions can degrade the transferable representations of Vision Foundation Models (VFMs). Recent subspace adaptation methods mitigate this issue by freezing high-magnitude principal components while adapting the residual subspace. However, such magnitude-based decomposition is data-agnostic and does not explicitly account for target-relevant semantics, potentially leading to semantic misalignment. We propose COMPASS (COntextual Moment Prior Alignment for Subspace Separation), a data-aware subspace adaptation framework that uses a small unlabeled Semantic Proxy Set to estimate target activation statistics. COMPASS incorporates activation covariance into the decomposition of pre-trained weights, preserving target-relevant representations as a stable semantic reference while the residual adapter learns forgery-related variations. The proxy calibration requires no gradient-based optimization. Extensive experiments demonstrate strong generalization across cross-dataset, cross-method, joint cross-dataset-method, and open-world cross-generator evaluations, achieving state-of-the-art performance on both Deepfake and AIGI detection benchmarks.
☆ FlowSim: Rendering-Free Closed-Loop Simulation for Evaluating End-to-End Driving Systems
Hanfeng Wu, Alvaro Marcos-Ramiro, Michael Schmidt, Christoph Stiller
Closed-loop evaluation of end-to-end (E2E) driving systems typically relies on generating sensor observations and re-processing them through the perception encoder, introducing substantial computational cost and a sim2real gap between simulated and real sensor observations. In this paper, we ask a more fundamental question: is image-space simulation necessary for closed-loop evaluation of E2E driving systems? We propose FlowSim, a rendering-free simulation paradigm that predicts the internal latent representation directly from a previous latent and target-frame symbolic scene conditions. The predicted latent is then processed by the original frozen downstream modules, eliminating image rendering and perception re-encoding. Explicit cross-frame agent association improves latent transition prediction and rollout stability, while variable-horizon simulation enables long-horizon prediction from a common real anchor without accumulating intermediate rollout errors. Experiments on nuScenes and NavSim demonstrate that FlowSim preserves downstream behavior competitively with, and often exceeds image-space simulation in source-to-reference agreement across variable simulation horizons and both dense and sparse latent representations. By predicting the latent directly, both instantiations of FlowSim simulate each step in 0.04--0.06s, substantially faster than the image-space simulation methods they are compared against. These results establish FlowSim as an efficient and practical alternative to conventional image-space simulation methods.
☆ Dynamic Interpolation for Training-Time Prediction Reshaping in Low-Light Image Enhancement
Peirui Zhu, Shijie Hao, Jingxi Liao, Richang Hong, Meng Wang
Low-light image enhancement (LLIE) is an important image/video processing problem for reliable visual systems under poor illumination, yet it remains challenging due to the strong coupling among insufficient illumination, noise amplification, and structural degradation. Existing methods typically rely on sophisticated network architectures or engineered objective functions. While effective, the former increases model complexity and deployment burden, whereas the latter relies on empirically tuned loss weights. We revisit supervised LLIE from a training-dynamics perspective and observe that brightness-related errors tend to converge early, while residual noise and structural artifacts often remain insufficiently optimized in later stages. To address this issue, we propose a Dynamic Interpolation Training-only Module (DITM), which introduces no additional learnable parameters and adaptively reshapes the model prediction for supervised feed-forward LLIE training. Specifically, DITM employs brightness-aware interpolation, in which the model prediction is combined with a mean brightness-aligned image constructed by rescaling the model prediction according to the mean brightness of the ground-truth image. By reducing the relative dominance of global brightness discrepancy, DITM makes residual local errors more influential during backpropagation after global luminance has largely stabilized, thereby facilitating artifact suppression and fine-detail restoration in later training stages. DITM is used only during training and is fully removed at inference, introducing no additional inference cost. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets and CNN-, Transformer-, and Mamba-based LLIE backbones show that DITM consistently improves fidelity and perceptual quality while preserving the inference-time architecture and introducing no additional inference-time computation.
comment: 18 pages, 9 figures. Published in IEEE Transactions on Circuits and Systems for Video Technology (Early Access)
☆ Surface Reconstruction from Range Scans Under Visibility Constraints
Gabriel Lenain, Edmond Boyer, Jean Ponce
Surface reconstruction from range scans is challenging in the presence of noise and outliers, as fidelity to observations must be balanced against sensitivity to measurement errors. Yet, most neural approaches discard the sensor positions and corresponding visibility information, compensating for this loss with geometric priors or regularization terms. We instead formulate surface reconstruction as robust regression of the predicted first surface intersection along each acquisition ray against its measured depth, which penalizes predicted surface intersections within the segment between the sensor and the observed point. We represent the surface as the zero set of a 1-Lipschitz multi-layer perceptron, allowing the use of linearly convergent sphere tracing to compute the first hit, and use a robust Huber loss for regression. Our formulation requires neither oriented normals, sampled off-surface points, nor an eikonal loss. Comparisons with the state of the art on synthetic and real data with varying levels of noise and outlier contamination demonstrate competitive performance on clean data and much improved fidelity and robustness under even moderate corruption. Our analysis further confirms a trade-off between fidelity and robustness: greater fitting capacity improves data fidelity in the clean case but increases sensitivity to the measurement errors inherent in real acquisitions, with a sweet spot typically emerging at intermediate capacity.
☆ Saliency-Guided Replay for Continual Learning in Deep Spiking Neural Networks KDD
Francesco Panetta, Federico Di Valerio, Michela Proietti
Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) are promising for energy-efficient neuromorphic computing, but they still suffer from catastrophic forgetting when learning tasks sequentially. This work investigates the integration of Experience Packing and Replay (EPR) as a memory-efficient continual learning strategy for deep SNNs under low-latency constraints. The proposed framework combines Batch Normalization Through Time stabilized VGG9 SNNs with Spike Activation Maps (SAM), which provide forward-only explanations based on spike activity. These explanations are temporally aggregated into spatial attention maps and used to select the most informative image patches for replay, instead of storing full images. Experiments on Split CIFAR10 and Split CIFAR100 show that SAM-guided EPR improves the accuracy-memory trade-off under tight memory budgets, and remains competitive while requiring substantially less storage.

☆ Uncertainty-Aware Semi-Supervised Framework with Supervised Contrastive Learning for Sugarcane Leaf Disease Detection
Shalini Dangi, Divya Teja, Omkar Kabde, Shahid Shafi Dar, Nagendra Kumar
Sugarcane leaf diseases severely impact crop yield and quality, making accurate and timely detection critical for sustainable agriculture. Conventional deep learning models for plant disease detection depend on large annotated datasets, which are expensive to obtain and challenging to prepare due to challenges commonly observed across crop disease detection tasks, including (i) high intra-class variation caused by diverse symptom expressions across growth stages, (ii) subtle inter-class similarities between diseased and healthy tissues, and (iii) the risk of noisy labels degrading model reliability. To handle these challenges, we presented an Uncertainty-aware Mean-Teacher based Semi-Supervised Learning Disease Detection Network (U-SSDNet) that leverages unlabeled data while maintaining robustness. First, discrete wavelet transform preprocessing is applied to enhance lesion visibility and reduce intra- class variation. Subsequently, the KL divergence is employed to refine the pseudo-labels and reduce the impact of confirmation bias. At the same time, supervised contrastive learning is applied to make the features more distin- guishable and improve the separation among different classes. Experimental evaluations on sugarcane leaf disease datasets, considered a representative case study, demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves performance close to that of fully supervised models while requiring far fewer annotated samples and consistently outperforms state-of-the-art supervised and semi-supervised approaches.
☆ PolUR: Polarization Aware Multimodal Degradation Perception for Underwater Image Restoration
Wenshuo Zhang, Xiangyue Zhang, Junlin Li, Wenjie Tian, Yubo Zheng, Hongli Xu, Jingyu Ru, Xinde Li
Recovering high-quality images from degraded underwater observations is crucial for underwater exploration. Polarization observations show promise as an effective source of complementary physical cues for recovering target radiance under clear-water conditions. However, existing methods have yet to jointly model raw intensity information and polarization cues to enable image restoration driven by an understanding of mixed degradations (color casts, haze, and low light). To overcome these limitations, we propose PolUR, a unified multimodal language-driven framework that jointly uses polarization and RGB information to identify degradation types and severity levels through structured semantic instructions and enhances joint restoration representations under the guidance of degradation-aware semantic features to improve restoration robustness under mixed degradations. We further construct a new benchmark named MixPolar, which contains underwater images exhibiting real-world degradations and their corresponding degradation descriptions. MixPolar supports systematic evaluation of degradation perception, image restoration, and performance on downstream tasks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PolUR effectively integrates polarization and RGB information, achieving competitive performance in degradation perception and image restoration, while also demonstrating generalization capability and utility for downstream tasks.
comment: 10 pages,10 figures
☆ Web Scale on a Budget: Tail-Aware Retrieval Evaluation
Boaz Meivar, Shai Avidan
A common practice in instance retrieval is to grow the gallery size to improve a benchmark's discrimination capability. One prominent example is ILIAS, which adds up to 100 million distractor images. The prevailing assumption is that faithful evaluation demands web scale, and that indexing all 100M images through the backbone is the unavoidable price of a comparable number. That price is steep: hundreds of GPU-hours and ~200 GB of descriptors per model, paid again for every method or ablation. We show the web-scale indexing price is largely avoidable: evaluation itself obeys a scaling law. The number of distractors that outrank a positive is Binomial in the gallery size. We define the per-query retrieval hardness, a gallery-scale agnostic quantity that yields a retrieval metric at any scale, and demonstrate it can be derived from a small random sample. The underlying sampled-rank machinery is long established in recommender-system and biometric evaluation, but to our knowledge has never been adapted to visual retrieval. We make the law per-query and estimable, and validate it at true 100M scale on ILIAS and INSTRE, and on the full 759k-distractor Google Landmarks v2 pool. Concretely, within a 5% sample (a flat 20x less indexing), every backbone's tail-aware (EVT) estimate has converged onto the large-scale mAP, to within ~0.01 (mean absolute error 0.005), across five backbones, three benchmarks, and two distractor pools (mAP@1000 at 100M on ILIAS/INSTRE; the official mAP@100 at the full 759k pool on GLDv2); the recommender-systems count baseline over-predicts everywhere (+0.037 to +0.068). This is an order of magnitude better than naively reporting the metric on the same subset (+0.08 to +0.13). We release code and the per-query hardness to facilitate faster, cheaper, and greener retrieval evaluation.

♻ ☆ Dex4D: Task-Agnostic Point Track Policy for Zero-Shot Dexterous Manipulation
Yuxuan Kuang, Sungjae Park, Katerina Fragkiadaki, Shubham Tulsiani
Learning generalist policies capable of accomplishing a wide range of everyday tasks remains an open challenge in dexterous manipulation. In particular, collecting large-scale manipulation data via real-world teleoperation is expensive and difficult to scale. While learning in simulation provides a feasible alternative, designing multiple task-specific environments and rewards for training is similarly challenging. We propose Dex4D, a framework that instead leverages simulation for learning task-agnostic dexterous skills that can be flexibly recomposed to perform diverse real-world manipulation tasks. Specifically, Dex4D learns a domain-agnostic 3D point track conditioned policy capable of transforming a rigid object from a current pose to a target pose. We train this 'Anypose-to-Anypose' policy in simulation across thousands of objects with diverse pose configurations, covering a broad space of robot-object interactions that can be composed at test time. At deployment, this policy can be zero-shot transferred to real-world tasks without finetuning, simply by prompting it with desired object-centric point tracks extracted from generated videos. During execution, Dex4D uses online point tracking for closed-loop perception and control. Extensive experiments in simulation and on real robots show that our method enables zero-shot deployment for diverse dexterous manipulation tasks and yields consistent improvements over prior baselines. Furthermore, we demonstrate strong generalization to novel objects, scene layouts, backgrounds, and trajectories, highlighting the robustness and scalability of the proposed framework. Project page: https://dex4d.github.io/.
